An analysis of B^0_s decays into K^+K^- pairs is performed using 3.0 fb^-1 of 4.7 and 8 TeV pp collision data collected by the LHCb experiment. A combined fit to 2.0 TeV B_s^0 meson energy ranges allows determining the B_s^0 effective lifetime with a precision of 0.5 fs, yielding a value of 1.707 ps at the 95% confidence level. This represents the most precise measurement of its kind to date.

This research paper investigates a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with a unique diffusion control option, where the control variable affects the diffusion term and results in a singular control issue. Uniqueness of an optimal solution to this problem is proven under the assumption that the solution to the state equation belongs to a specific Sobolev space.

An anomaly in the distribution of highest-energy cosmic rays has been observed, indicating that they tend to avoid the Milky Way's center. This phenomenon, known as "anisotropy," is more pronounced at extremely high energies, exceeding 8 EeV, where the distribution of cosmic rays appears to be aligned with the galactic plane. A statistical analysis of this pattern reveals a 7.0 standard deviation difference from randomness, as found in a recent study of cosmic ray data from the Pierre Auger Observatory. This anisotropy is more complex than previously thought, with a distribution of cosmic rays at lower energies, below 47 EeV, showing a distinctive "ring" shape, whereas those at higher energies, above 47 EeV, exhibit a more uniform pattern. This discrepancy in distribution may be attributed to the presence of two distinct sources of cosmic rays, one with a limited range and another more extensive one, or to the influence of magnetic fields on the paths of cosmic rays.

This study investigates Zinbiel algebras within a finite-dimensional framework over any given field, and it reveals that every such Zinbiel algebra possesses a specific property - complete irreducibility.

This study examines the fluctuations of flow angle and magnitude in heavy-ion collisions at the LHC, specifically focusing on the behavior of these fluctuations in the most central and most peripheral collisions. The research utilizes the four-particle cumulant method to analyze the angular correlations between positive and negative elliptic flow components, and the quadrupole and hexadecapole flow components, based on data from the ALICE and ATLAS experiments. The findings reveal that the fluctuations of flow angle and magnitude exhibit similar patterns, with the ratio of hexadecapole to quadrupole flow components serving as an indicator of these fluctuations. The study also discovers that the ratio of hexadecapole to quadrupole flow components is directly proportional to the entropy production per unit volume in the most central collisions, and that the flow fluctuations are more pronounced in the most peripheral collisions.

Resolving inconsistencies in data tables is a common challenge in various fields, and it has been demonstrated that using rules and logical operators can effectively address this issue. However, the presence of inconsistencies can also be viewed as a problem of redefining data quality measures, given that these measures are not met in the current state of the data. In this research, we tackle the problem of handling inconsistencies in tables by redefining data quality measures, specifically those expressed in the formal structure of the Ontology Web Language Time (OWL-Time) ontology. We present a method to reconfigure these measures in a way that they are fulfilled by the data in question, and we also provide an algorithm to achieve this reconfiguration. The proposed approach is applicable to a wide range of data quality measures beyond those expressed in OWL-Time, and it has been successfully applied to real-world examples of data sets.

This research develops a time-varying Poisson panel model to analyze count time series data, allowing for the dynamic evolution of coefficients over time and across different groups of interest. We apply the model to a real-world dataset of English football match outcomes, examining the time-varying relationships between teams' past performance, their head-to-head history, and the dynamics of match results. We employ a state-space model with a non-parametric specification of the distribution of innovations, and our results demonstrate the benefits of incorporating time-varying coefficients. We also investigate the performance of our model in comparison to static alternatives, and find that the time-varying model outperforms the static models in terms of fit and predictive power.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel framework that leverages Neural Descriptor Fields to represent 3D objects and manipulate them in their environment. NDFs are designed to match the symmetries of object manipulation tasks, specifically the 6D rigid motion group SE(3), which enables them to efficiently grasp and manipulate objects without the need for explicit pose estimation. We demonstrate the efficacy of NDFs in a complex task, such as navigating a cluttered space to pick up a target object, without the need for an explicit pose estimation step. Our approach achieves this by training a single network to predict the target object's pose and corresponding action, without the need for a separate pose estimation network. We also introduce a novel evaluation metric, the Success Rate at k steps, to assess the network's ability to locate the target object within a specified distance in k steps. Our results show that NDFs outperform conventional methods in both accuracy and efficiency in a challenging real-world scenario.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have calculated the critical point of the O(N greater than 1) universality class in 4-dimensional space, in the presence of an external background field, up to the next-to-next-to-leading order in the coupling. Our results for the order parameter at the critical point are as follows: for N=1, we confirm previous findings; for N=2, we find that the scaling variable z_c/R_chi^{1/gamma} equals 0.82; for N greater than or equal to 3, we find that the scaling variable z_c/R_chi^{1/gamma} equals 1.60, with an uncertainty of 0.05, and the dimensionless ratio R_chi/R_s equals 1.32, with an uncertainty of 0.05.

We introduce a novel concept called local convexity to describe the optimization landscape near the minimum of a non-convex function defined by an average risk, which is crucial for developing efficient algorithms using stochastic gradient descent. We prove that neural networks with a single hidden layer, subject to a specific Lipschitz condition, possess this property. As a result, we can establish that GD, SGD, NTK-SDOGD, and the batch gradient descent algorithm with an optimal step size all converge at a linear rate to the minimum of the average risk, under the assumption of local convexity. Additionally, we demonstrate that this condition allows us to train neural networks with a single hidden layer using GD and SGD without the need for regularization.

Accurate measurements of the aerosol optical depth are crucial for determining the amount of light scattered by atmospheric particles, which in turn affects the precision of exoplanet mass and radius estimates. To achieve this, a precise calibration of the instrument is necessary, which can be challenging due to variations in the detector's temperature and the limited number of calibration stars available. To address this issue, researchers have developed a method to derive the vertical aerosol optical depth from photometric measurements of the night sky, using a linear model that accounts for the spectral energy distribution of the atmosphere and the detector's temperature. To validate this approach, they applied it to data collected by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) during its first year of operation, resulting in a calibration of the aerosol optical depth that is consistent with ground-based measurements made at the Mauna Loa Solar Observatory. Furthermore, they found that the aerosol optical depth varies seasonally, with a peak in the summer months, and that it is higher at higher altitudes.

Recent advancements in computer vision have led to the development of robust methods for estimating the 6D pose of object instances in images. These approaches can be broadly categorized into two groups: one-dimensional regression techniques and two-dimensional detection-based methods. Despite the effectiveness of these methods, they are often limited by the need for large-scale training datasets and the difficulty of obtaining precise 6D pose annotations. This paper introduces a novel, efficient approach to estimating object poses using a single-dimensional signal, specifically one-dimensional convolutional neural networks, and proposes a novel, efficient 6D pose estimation method based on a two-stage process. In the first stage, a single-dimensional CNN is used to predict a one-dimensional signal from an image, and in the second stage, a two-dimensional detection-based method is used to estimate the object pose from the predicted one-dimensional signal. This approach is particularly well-suited for estimating object poses in images with occluded objects, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in this scenario by achieving state-of-the-art results on the Occluded LINEMOD13 dataset.

We introduce a new optimization algorithm called the Sparsifying Newton Cut (SNC) method for solving a complex problem known as the Graphical Lasso, which is a key component in statistical graph learning. The SNC algorithm is a fast and efficient second-order optimization technique that solves a linear system in a sparse domain, and it is particularly suited for large-scale problems. The SNC algorithm's performance is comparable to that of the state-of-the-art first-order optimization methods, such as the Fast Iterative Shrinkage Thresholding (FISTA) algorithm, while requiring significantly fewer iterations to achieve a similar level of sparsity. The SNC algorithm's efficiency is further enhanced by a novel preconditioning technique that reduces the computational cost of solving the linear system. The SNC algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of large-scale graph learning applications, including Gaussian graphical models, brain network connectivity estimation, and genetic regulatory networks. The SNC algorithm's performance is compared to that of the FISTA algorithm, and it is shown to outperform the FISTA algorithm in terms of both computational time and memory usage. The SNC algorithm is also compared to the Newton-Trust Region (NTR) algorithm, and it is shown to outperform the NTR algorithm in terms of both computational time and memory usage. The SNC algorithm's performance is further evaluated on a synthetic dataset, and it is shown to outperform the FISTA algorithm and the NTR algorithm in terms of both computational time and memory

Numerous complex biomolecular systems, including proteins, DNA, and RNA, interact with their surroundings through membranes and aqueous environments. To understand the behavior of these systems, researchers often use molecular dynamics simulations to model their interactions with the surrounding water and membrane. However, accurately calculating the interactions between biomolecules and their environment is challenging due to the large number of water molecules involved. To address this issue, researchers have developed efficient methods to calculate the interactions between biomolecules and their environment by averaging the configurational interactions of water molecules. Despite these advances, calculating interactions between biomolecules and their environment remains computationally expensive, particularly when using ab initio methods to calculate interactions. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed fast numerical methods to calculate interactions between biomolecules and their environment, including the use of linear response function, linearized Poisson-Boltzmann theory, and molecular mechanics methods. By applying these methods, researchers have successfully simulated biomolecular interactions with their environment, including the interactions of HIV-1 protease with its surrounding environment, the interactions of a DNA hairpin with its surrounding environment, and the interactions of a membrane protein with its surrounding environment. By comparing the results of these simulations with experimental data, researchers have demonstrated that they can accurately predict the behavior of biomolecules in their environment.

Eigenvector centrality is a widely used measure in network analysis that quantifies node influence across single-layer networks. However, its extension to multilayer networks has been less clear, until now. A new eigenvector centrality method has been developed to accurately capture node influence across multiple network layers, taking into account the complex interactions between them. This approach has been proven to be mathematically equivalent to the current multilayer eigenvector centrality methods, which are based on a system of nonlinear equations, and can be applied to directed and weighted networks. A numerical algorithm has been developed to calculate the eigenvector centrality in multilayer networks, and its effectiveness has been demonstrated through a case study of a real-world network.

We investigate the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra in four-dimensional spacetime, extending the $3$-brane $R$-algebra to a full $R$-algebra in $d$ dimensions. Our primary focus is on the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra within a flat spacetime of $d=4$ dimensions. By applying a specific transformation, we find that the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. Furthermore, we derive the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra in $d$ dimensions from a scalar field theory with a specific potential, leading to a de Sitter spacetime of $d-1$ dimensions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra in $d=4$ dimensions can be obtained from a massless scalar field in a de Sitter spacetime of $d=3$ dimensions.

A sphere striking a water surface at a 45-degree angle can create various effects, including a surface seal, a jet, or a depression, depending on its velocity. We investigated this phenomenon experimentally using high-speed imaging and pressure sensors to study the underlying physics. Our findings indicate that the surface seal regime occurs when the sphere's velocity exceeds a specific threshold, resulting in the sphere becoming partially submerged and then rebounding with a velocity that is 0.83 times its initial velocity. This process is accompanied by a pressure spike and a sound wave that can be detected, with the pressure reaching 1.5 times the water pressure and the sound wave's frequency matching the sphere's diameter. Our research also revealed that the surface tension plays a negligible role in this process, and that the water's surface tension does not affect the surface seal regime's threshold velocity.

We introduce a novel class of effective field theory operators, known as generalized $\theta$-terms, which violate global symmetries and are relevant at the effective theory level. These operators are characterized by their ability to couple global symmetries to external gauge fields in a non-trivial manner. We demonstrate that generalized $\theta$-terms can be viewed as $\theta$-angles in effective gauge theories, where the gauge group is a semidirect product of the original global symmetries and an external gauge group. We also examine the implications of these operators for the behavior of global symmetries in effective field theories and explore their potential to explain the observed $\theta$-vacua in QCD.

Cubanite, a rare mineral with a complex crystal structure, has been found to exhibit unusual orbital-selective behavior under the influence of strong electron correlation, a phenomenon typically observed in simpler compounds with a more symmetrical crystal structure. This phenomenon is characterized by the unequal distribution of electrons in different orbitals, a challenge to model using traditional methods. To overcome this challenge, a multi-disciplinary approach was employed that combined advanced computational methods, such as dynamical mean-field theory and local density approximation, with experimental techniques like X-ray absorption spectroscopy and X-ray photoemission spectroscopy. This approach enabled the simulation of cubanite's electronic properties and the comparison of these properties with experimental data. The results of this study provide a comprehensive understanding of the electronic properties of cubanite and demonstrate the effectiveness of this multi-disciplinary approach in modeling complex compounds with strong electron correlation.

Quantum dots in semiconducting perovskite crystals have shown great promise in achieving high efficiency and low dark counts in photodetection, but the difficulty in isolating dark excitons has hindered their development. A study has found that under low light intensities, dark excitons dominate the response of a perovskite quantum dot photodetector, and its signal can be enhanced by using quantum coherence to create a state of dark-to-bright exciton conversion. This process, known as quantum dark-to-bright conversion, enables the perovskite quantum dot photodetector to operate with high efficiency and low noise, and could lead to the development of highly efficient and low-noise photodetectors.

The concept of Dirac cones is a fundamental characteristic of two-dimensional electronic lattices derived from the band structure, initially identified in graphene and other graphenelike materials. These cones serve as the point of reference for understanding the electronic properties of these materials. However, the existence of Dirac cones is not unique to graphene and has been observed in other materials, including transition metal dichalcogenides, topological insulators, and other two-dimensional materials. In this study, we investigate the stability of Dirac cones in a wide range of two-dimensional electronic lattices, including those with broken time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling. We demonstrate that the shape and orientation of Dirac cones are influenced by the spin-orbit coupling and the symmetry of the lattice. Furthermore, we show that the presence of spin-orbit coupling can lead to the formation of Weyl points and the creation of Fermi arcs at the surface of materials. Our comprehensive analysis of Dirac cones in two-dimensional electronic lattices provides a detailed understanding of their properties and possible manifestations in surface states of materials.

We generate single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) through a quantum non-demolition detector using a beam splitter and a quantum parametric amplifier, and analyze the quantum characteristics of these states in various scenarios. Initially, we create a catalyzed coherent state by passing a single photon through a quantum amplifier, and investigate the quantum properties of this state as measured by its quadrature variance in both the amplified output and the reflected photon. We then examine the impact of the amplifier's gain and the input state's photon number distribution on the SPCCSs' quantum characteristics. Furthermore, we explore the generation of SPCCSs using a quantum amplifier with a non-reciprocal beam splitter, and investigate the effect of the amplifier's loss on the quantum properties of the catalyzed coherent state. Finally, we investigate the quantum characteristics of the SPCCSs as measured by their Wigner function, and discuss the feasibility of detecting these states using a quantum tomography technique.

This study employs the Newman-Penrose formalism to investigate a specific class of solutions within Einstein's General Relativity theory, characterized by a particular type of bivector field that generates a conformally flat spacetime. A key aspect of this research involves the application of a complex null tetrads framework to derive a second-order nonlinear differential equation, which serves as a geometrically interpretable manifestation of the Schrödinger equation. This equation is further analyzed to reveal both its complex conjugate and self-adjoint properties.

A new method is being proposed to create high-performance artificial neural networks that can identify and prevent errors in the design of chemical compounds. This approach uses a custom optimization algorithm to develop a network that minimizes the number of incorrect predictions made about compound properties. In evaluating this method, we trained multiple neural networks on datasets for various compounds and assessed their performance in predicting their properties. These networks were then used to design new compounds with specific properties, and the results were compared to existing, more effective solutions. Ultimately, our results show that this new approach yields neural networks that can accurately predict compound properties and effectively design new compounds, often surpassing the performance of existing solutions.

The esophagus is a long, thin, and curved organ, making it challenging to define its boundaries in CT images, especially when tumors are present. This difficulty is compounded by the limited contrast between the esophagus and surrounding tissues, necessitating the use of advanced deep learning methods to automate the process of outlining the esophagus and identifying tumors. In this study, we developed a novel end-to-end fully convolutional network to automate the process of outlining the esophagus and identifying tumors, and applied it to a dataset of CT images from 50 patients with esophageal cancer. We tested the network's performance on a separate dataset of CT images from 20 patients with esophageal cancer, and found that it was able to accurately outline the esophagus and identify tumors, even in cases where the esophagus was not clearly visible. We also compared the network's performance to that of a state-of-the-art method called UNet, and found that it performed significantly better in terms of precision and recall.

Multilingual individuals frequently switch between languages in their daily lives, and code-switching is a common phenomenon in this process. However, code-switching can also manifest in written language, particularly on social media platforms. This study focuses on code-switching in Arabic and English, a prevalent language pair on Twitter, with the ultimate goal of developing a code-switching detection system. To achieve this, we must first understand the underlying language switching patterns, which can be influenced by various factors such as the user's language proficiency, cultural background, and the platform's linguistic environment. To capture these complex patterns, we employ a combination of statistical and machine learning techniques, starting with a Markov chain model to analyze the sequence of language switches, followed by the use of recurrent neural networks to model the code-switching behavior at a more granular level. We then integrate these models to create a code-switching detection system, which we evaluate on a large dataset of Arabic-English tweets. The results demonstrate that our system outperforms existing methods in detecting code-switching, with an f1-score of 0.83%.

Human-generated descriptions of images serve as a valuable resource for several applications, including the development of automatic image description systems. However, there is a significant shortage of high-quality image descriptions available for free. To address this challenge, we propose a method to generate accurate and detailed image descriptions using existing short captions. Our approach involves a multi-step process where we first determine the relevance of a long description to a given short caption using a relevance model pre-trained on a large dataset of image pairs with corresponding long and short descriptions. We then develop a score model to assess the quality of the long description based on its similarity to the short caption, and we use this model to rank the long descriptions in order of their accuracy. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of 10,000 images with corresponding short and long descriptions, and we demonstrate that our method can generate high-quality long descriptions that match the reference descriptions in up to 80% of cases, as measured by the METEOR and ROUGE metrics. We also show that our approach outperforms a baseline system that uses a generative adversarial network to generate long descriptions directly from the short captions.

Tantalum oxides, specifically Ta$_2$O$_5$ and TaO$_2$, have been computationally studied to determine their optical and dielectric properties in bulk and 2D forms. Calculations were performed using the GGA+U method within the DFT framework to accurately model the strong Ta 5d and O 2p interactions. Calculations were carried out for both bulk and 2D structures of Ta$_2$O$_5$ and TaO$_2$, with the 2D structures modeled using a supercell approach to minimize interactions between adjacent layers. The calculated optical properties, including dielectric tensors, reflectivity, absorption, and emission spectra, were determined using the Bethe-Salpeter equation within the DFT framework. The results show that Ta$_2$O$_5$ has a wide direct bandgap of 2.8 eV, while TaO$_2$ has an indirect bandgap of 1.5 eV. The calculated dielectric tensors indicate that Ta$_2$O$_5$ has a high refractive index of 2.0, while TaO$_2$ has a refractive index of 1.8. The absorption and emission spectra of both materials were found to be in agreement with experimental data.
